title: Indian-American Engineer Arvind Raman Confirmed as 18th Director of NIST
excerpt: The former Purdue engineering dean now leads America's premier standards and technology agency, overseeing AI, quantum, and cybersecurity research.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Arvind Raman was sworn in as NIST's 18th Director on June 30, 2026.
  • He was confirmed by the Senate on May 18 with a 46-43 vote.
  • Raman oversees research in AI, quantum tech, cybersecurity, and manufacturing.
  • Previously, he was Dean of Engineering at Purdue University since 2023.
  • Raman's appointment highlights the growing influence of Indian-Americans in federal science.
  • Arvind Raman, an Indian-American engineer from Purdue University, was sworn in as the 18th Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology on June 30, 2026
  • Raman was confirmed by the U.S. Senate on May 18 after being nominated by President Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick
  • As NIST Director, Raman oversees research and standards development in AI, quantum technology, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and biotechnology
  • Before NIST, Raman served as the John A. Edwardson Dean of Engineering at Purdue, with research focused on atomic force microscopy, biomechanics, and electronics manufacturing

From Purdue to America's Standards Agency

Arvind Raman was sworn in on June 30, 2026, as the 18th Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, becoming the latest Indian-American to lead a major U.S. federal science agency. The appointment places him at the helm of one of America's oldest and most consequential scientific institutions, overseeing work that spans artificial intelligence safety standards, quantum computing, cybersecurity frameworks, and advanced manufacturing.

Raman was confirmed by the Senate on May 18 in a 46-43 vote that largely split along party lines. His nomination by President Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick drew on his long track record at Purdue University, where he rose from assistant professor in 2000 to become the John A. Edwardson Dean of Engineering in 2023.

Leadership Transition at NIST
2000
Raman joins Purdue University as assistant professor.
2012
Raman becomes Robert V. Adams Professor of Engineering.
2023
Raman appointed Dean of Engineering at Purdue.
May 18, 2026
Raman confirmed by Senate in a 46-43 vote.
June 30, 2026
Raman sworn in as 18th Director of NIST.

"NIST is one of America's most important science institutions thanks to its unique mission and the expertise of its employees. I look forward to maximizing NIST's ability to accelerate American innovation through partnerships with industry, entrepreneurs and other stakeholders."

— Arvind Raman, NIST Director

A Career Built on Precision

Raman's academic career has been defined by work at the intersection of physics and engineering. His research focused on atomic force microscopy — the technology used to image and manipulate materials at the nanometer scale — as well as human biomechanics and electronics manufacturing. He collaborated extensively with NIST researchers on nanotechnology projects throughout his career, making the directorship a natural progression.

At Purdue, Raman earned multiple awards for teaching and was appointed the Robert V. Adams Professor of Engineering in 2012. The university's engineering program is consistently ranked among the top ten in the United States.

NIST's Critical Role in Innovation
›Founded in 1901, NIST supports American measurement science.
›NIST's work impacts sectors like cybersecurity and AI safety.
›Central to CHIPS Act implementation and post-quantum cryptography.
›NIST collaborates with industry and stakeholders for innovation.

What NIST Does and Why It Matters

Founded in 1901, NIST sits under the Department of Commerce and serves as the backbone of American measurement science and technical standards. Its work touches virtually every sector of the economy — from the cybersecurity framework used by thousands of organizations to the AI safety standards that will shape how machine learning systems are deployed. NIST's semiconductor research is central to the CHIPS Act implementation, and its quantum information science program is helping set the agenda for post-quantum cryptography.

Growing Indian-American Presence in Federal Science

Raman's appointment continues a pattern of Indian-origin scientists and technologists reaching the top ranks of U.S. federal agencies. His predecessors in similar roles include former CTO of the United States Aneesh Chopra and former NASA Deputy Administrator Shri Thanedar. For the Indian diaspora, these appointments represent both professional recognition and a deepening influence on the policies that govern technology, innovation, and competitiveness in America.
